summary: This informational RFC defines an IPv6 profile for 3GPP mobile devices that is a superset of the cellular host profile in RFC 7066. It covers both mobile hosts and mobile devices that can share their cellular connection with other nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of IPv6 features a phone should support, including when it shares its connection with other devices.

questions: what is an ipv6 profile for 3gpp mobile devices
subtitle: A checklist of IPv6 features a 3GPP phone, dongle or cellular router should support, including IPv4 access over IPv6-only networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile operators moving to IPv6-only networks found that many devices lacked working IPv6 and the means to still reach IPv4-only services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists numbered recommendations for cellular hosts (C_REC), devices that share their connection (L_REC) and critical services such as VoLTE (A_REC), building on RFC 7066.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational, independent-stream document that is not a standard. It gives operators one list to hand to device vendors.

today: RFC 7849 is an Informational document from the independent submission stream, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The IESG note points to RFC 7066 as the consensus-based IETF description of IPv6 for cellular hosts.

sections.title: Why a Mobile IPv6 Profile
sections.content:
The RFC argues that IPv6 deployment in 3GPP mobile networks is the only viable answer to IPv4 address exhaustion there. One hurdle operators perceive is the lack of working IPv6 in mobile devices. RFC 7066 already lists features for cellular hosts, but the authors add features that help IPv6-only deployments reach IPv4-only services.

The document has three stated goals: list the IPv6 features of a mobile device in one place (for both IPv6-only and dual-stack cases), help operators prepare device requirement lists for suppliers, and tell vendors what is needed for IPv6 connectivity and IPv4 service continuity over IPv6-only transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone companies want phones that work on the new address system. This paper puts all the needed features in one list so phone makers know what to build.

sections.title: Scope and Status of the Profile
sections.content:
The profile covers any node that connects directly to a 3GPP network, including GPRS and EPS. It is a superset of the profile in RFC 7066, which is itself a superset of IPv6 Node Requirements. Where the two conflict, for example on Neighbor Discovery, it follows RFC 7066. Machine-to-machine devices are out of scope.

The text says plainly that it is not a standard. Conformance is not required to claim conformance with IETF IPv6 standards, and supporting every item is not required in every deployment. The authors do believe that skipping relevant items, such as CLAT, may lead to a degraded level of service.

It also uses stronger language than RFC 7066 for Prefix Delegation, because cellular networks are increasingly an alternative to fixed networks for home services.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is advice, not a law. But the authors warn that leaving out important items can make the phone work worse.

sections.title: Connectivity Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 2 holds nine recommendations, C_REC#1 to C_REC#9. A cellular host must support both IPv6 and IPv4v6 PDP-Contexts, must request an IPv6 PDP-Context by default if it is IPv6-only, and an IPv4v6 one if it is dual-stack or does not know what its attached devices need. If the network refuses IPv4v6 but allows both single types, the host must open a second PDP-Context for the other family. If only one family is allowed it must not ask for the other.

The host must use Protocol Configuration Options (PCO) to learn DNS server addresses and must support IPv6-aware Traffic Flow Templates. If DNS information arrives by several channels, the order is PCO, then RA, then DHCPv6. It must also be configurable with separate home and roaming PDP types.

For IPv4 service continuity the host should learn the PREFIX64 and should implement the CLAT function, using it only when the network assigns no IPv4 address to the cellular interface. A host may also be configured to limit the PDP types for an APN.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone must be able to ask the network for the right kind of connection and know which helper to trust for directions. It also has a way to reach old websites even if the network only speaks the new language.

sections.title: Devices That Share Their Connection
sections.content:
Section 3 applies to cellular devices that provide connectivity to other devices, such as CE routers, smartphones or dongles with tethering. All devices behind them share one 2G, 3G or LTE connection.

Such a device must support Prefix Delegation and the Prefix Exclude Option for DHCPv6-based delegation, acting as a Requesting Router. That lets each LAN segment get its own /64. Because some networks lack Prefix Delegation, a device should also support sharing a /64 between LAN and WAN, to be used only when Prefix Delegation is not in use.

A cellular CE router must meet the requirements of RFC 7084. If the network advertises an MTU in Router Advertisements, the device should pass the same MTU to the LAN. The text notes that 3GPP TS 23.060 says a link MTU of 1358 octets prevents fragmentation between the device and the GGSN/PGW.
sections.plainLanguage: If your phone is a hotspot, it has to hand out address blocks to the gadgets that connect to it, like a landlord giving each room its own number.

sections.title: Advanced Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 4 targets critical services such as VoLTE and applies to mobile hosts. A host must support the ROHC RTP profile (0x0001) and the ROHC UDP profile (0x0002) for IPv6 so larger IPv6 headers waste less bandwidth.

A host should support the Port Control Protocol (PCP). The RFC cites measurements that keep-alive messages cost battery: at a 20 second interval 29 mA (2G) and 34 mA (3G), falling to 5.2 mA (2G) and 6.1 mA (3G) with no keep-alives. PCP also lets a host control NAT64 and firewall functions without application level gateways.

To keep DNSSEC validation working behind NAT64, the host should embed a DNS64 function in stub-resolver mode. A dual-stack host should prefer native IPv6 over translated paths and contact its IPv6 DNS server first.
sections.plainLanguage: These extras save phone battery and bandwidth and keep phone calls and safe website lookups working smoothly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7066 and RFC 6459 apply. A cellular CE router that meets RFC 7084 also inherits the security considerations of RFC 6092, including the warning that stateful filtering may reduce security and that the IETF makes no statement on whether it improves security overall.

The cellular host must be able to generate privacy-preserving IPv6 addresses, for example using RFC 7217. Tracking is still possible based on the first 64 bits of the address, so the network side may need additional measures.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone should not use an address that makes it easy to follow it around. But the first half of the address can still give clues.
